title: Relevance is the New Relationship Currency
summary: Generational research shows how financial institutions can make personalized banking more relevant, useful, and trusted across every life stage.
body_markdown:
## How financial institutions can use generational insights to deliver more personalized banking experiences


Banking leaders sit at a crossroads, scratching their heads trying to answer the question, “How can we better understand what our account holders need as their financial circumstances change?”


That sentiment surfaced as a desire among consumers as well in Alkami’s[2026 Generational Trends in Digital Banking Study](https://www.alkami.com/resources/research/2026-generational-trends-in-digital-banking-report/) . Specifically, 44% of digital banking Americans wish their primary financial provider did a better job anticipating their financial needs and goals.


Knowing your account holders is one part of the relationship circle. Demonstrating that understanding as their needs evolve is what makes each interaction relevant and improves loyalty over time.


The[digital banking platform](https://www.alkami.com/digital-banking-solutions/) has become a defining part of the financial relationship, with 85% of respondents saying the digital experience quality is important when selecting a new primary provider. Every login, alert, recommendation, and service interaction is an opportunity to demonstrate an understanding of what matters to the individual and help them move forward with confidence.


### Why generational relevance starts with the users’ end goal in mind


It’s tempting to think of generational preferences for[personalized banking](https://www.alkami.com/blog/why-personalized-banking-matters-a-guide-for-banks-credit-unions/) primarily in terms of channels. Younger generations prefer digital, older generations prefer human interaction. However, the research tells a more nuanced story. Financial institutions need to have an understanding of the financial goals, pressures, and expectations behind each interaction, then use this context to deliver an experience that feels useful.


Alkami’s 2026 research reveals distinct patterns among each generation’s preferences when it comes to their ideal financial provider and digital banking platform:


- Generation Z seeks clarity.
- Millennials seek coordination.
- Generation X seeks control.
- Baby Boomers seek protection.


These aren’t rigid definitions of individual preferences. They offer a starting point for understanding how financial needs and expectations evolve. Seventy-six percent of study participants say the digital banking experience reflects how much their financial institution cares about its account holders.


This serves as a powerful reminder that technology decisions have a direct influence on how people perceive their financial relationships. The goal is to use data and technology to make each interaction feel more relevant to the person behind the account.


For a closer look at how financial priorities and expectations differ across generations,[read this blog](https://www.alkami.com/blog/generational-trends-a-playbook-for-financial-institutions/) . Understanding those differences can help financial institutions identify where guidance, personalization, and human support may have the greatest impact.


Across all four generations, one principle remains consistent…


Relevance comes from understanding what someone needs in the moment, rather than assuming everyone in a generation needs the same thing.


### What the research reveals about the personalization gap


Financial institutions are making progress with personalization, but account holders aren’t experiencing that progress equally. According to the study, 47% of digital banking consumers believe product recommendations from their primary financial institution have improved over the past year. Relevancy has seen incremental improvements when benchmarked year-over-year, with 44% of consumers reporting they felt their recommendations were more tailored in 2025, compared to 41% in 2024.


However, perception varies by provider type. Among consumers using online-only providers, 51% say recommendations have improved, compared with 50% at major national[banks](https://www.alkami.com/banks/) and just 38% at regional and community financial institutions. That 13-percentage-point gap between online-only providers and regional and community financial institutions represents a meaningful opportunity to improve product recommendations or next steps in their journey.


Regional and community financial institutions have built their reputations on personal service, local knowledge, and long-standing relationships. The next opportunity is to bring those same advantages into digital experiences.


The need goes deeper than product recommendations. The research found 51% of participants say managing their finances takes an emotional toll, while 52% look to their financial institution for guidance. People want help making sense of their financial lives. They want to know what to do next, how to make progress toward their goals, and where to turn when decisions become complicated.


A timely explanation, useful next step, or relevant recommendation can make those decisions feel less overwhelming. This is where personalization becomes a relationship strategy. When account holders feel understood and supported, financial institutions have more opportunities to earn trust and strengthen relationships over time.


### How financial institutions can turn generational insights into personalized banking experiences


Financial institutions can use this understanding of generational differences to improve each next interaction. By combining broader generational patterns with individual behaviors, preferences, and financial circumstances, they can deliver more timely, useful experiences.


Consider prioritizing these four opportunities.


### 1. Make onboarding relevant from the start


The account opening experience is an early opportunity to demonstrate a financial institution understands how people want to manage their finances. According to the research, 68% of Americans using digital banking prefer a mobile device when opening a new account online. A mobile-friendly experience is essential, but flexibility is important, too. Applicants should be able to move between devices or channels without losing their progress, whether they begin on a phone and finish on a computer or at a branch. Simple, intuitive onboarding helps establish confidence at the beginning of the relationship and creates a foundation for future engagement.


### 2. Make product or service recommendations timely and explainable


More recommendations don’t necessarily create a better experience. What’s key is whether the recommendation makes sense for the account holder’s circumstances. Consider an account holder working toward a savings goal, someone building credit, or a retiree managing money across multiple accounts. Each may benefit from a different kind of guidance.


By using behavioral insights alongside broader generational context, financial institutions can identify opportunities to provide recommendations that are relevant to an individual’s financial priorities.


Consider an account holder who receives a promotion for a business loan when they don’t own a business. Instead of thinking their financial institution understands their needs, they may be annoyed. Rather than increasing brand loyalty, the relationship may instead suffer. On the other hand, if an account holder recently purchased a car but didn’t have the opportunity to shop for a loan outside of the dealership, an offer to refinance a car loan at a better rate may help build the relationship.


### 3. Connect 24/7 digital self-service with human support


Digital banking and human service should work together, with account holders able to move between channels as their support needs or challenges become more complex. Among Generation X (Gen X) respondents, 91% say phone support is important, while 87% prioritize online virtual assistance. Among Baby Boomers, 81% value convenient locations and 57% say access to knowledgeable staff matters most during a branch visit.


The experience should feel connected. If someone starts a conversation digitally and needs additional assistance, they shouldn’t have to repeat information or start over. Maintaining context across channels helps make service more convenient and reinforces the feeling that the financial institution understands the individual.


### 4. Use AI to solve specific account holder needs


Artificial intelligence (AI) has the potential to make financial experiences more useful, but account holders need to understand the benefit. Alkami’s research found just over half of digital banking consumers are comfortable with their financial data being processed by AI if it leads to a better experience. That comfort rises to 67% when AI is used to identify suspicious or fraudulent transactions and notify the account holder.


People are more receptive when they can see how AI technology benefits them. Financial institutions should use it when it addresses meaningful needs, whether it’s identifying unusual activity, explaining spending patterns, or helping someone understand their next financial step. The goal is to use AI with purpose, making the experience clearer, safer, or more helpful.


### How relevance fuels relationship growth


Account holders maintain relationships with an average of 3.3 to 3.7 financial institutions across generations, according to the study. That means a long-standing relationship doesn’t automatically translate into primary-provider status. Financial institutions have to continue demonstrating why they deserve a larger role in an account holder’s financial life. Every interaction creates another opportunity to earn the primary provider role.


Regional and community financial institutions already understand the importance of personal relationships. With the right combination of data, technology, and human insight, they can extend their personal understanding into the digital banking experiences account holders rely on every day.


By recognizing changing needs and responding with timely guidance, financial institutions can move from reacting to account holder requests toward helping people prepare for what’s next. Generational insights can point financial institutions in the right direction. Individual understanding is what makes the experience relevant.


In a world where account holders have more financial relationships and more choices than ever, delivering personalized banking may be one of the most actionable ways to nurture a lasting relationship.


### FAQs


1


What does personalized banking mean?


Personalized banking means using relevant information about an account holder’s needs, goals, behaviors, and circumstances to make digital experiences, guidance, and recommendations more useful.


2


Why does generational relevance matter in digital banking?


Generational research can reveal broad patterns in financial priorities and expectations. Used carefully, those patterns help financial institutions design more relevant experiences without treating age as a substitute for individual understanding.


3


How can financial institutions personalize the digital banking platform?


Financial institutions can personalize the digital banking platform by connecting account opening information, digital behavior, product data, engagement history, and service context to timely next steps and suggestions.


4


How can banks and credit unions personalize experiences without generalizing?


Use generation as context, not as a conclusion. Combine broad generational patterns with each account holder’s actual behavior, stated preferences, financial goals, and stage of life.


5


How does AI support personalized banking?


AI can support personalized banking when it solves a clear problem, such as helping account holders understand their finances, receive timely fraud alerts, or navigate a complex decision.
